title: 14. Voice Prompt Car with Espeak and Pico2Wave

sections.title: 14. Voice Prompt Car with Espeak and Pico2Wave

inlines.v: In this lesson, we'll use two built-in text-to-speech (TTS) engines on Raspberry Pi —
These two engines are both simple and run offline, but they sound quite different:
: very lightweight and fast, but the voice is robotic. You can adjust speed, pitch, and volume.
: produces a smoother and more natural voice than Espeak, but has fewer options to configure.
, and then build a "voice prompt car" that announces its actions before moving.
Espeak is a lightweight TTS engine included in Raspberry Pi OS. Its voice sounds robotic, but it is highly configurable: you can adjust volume, pitch, speed, and more.
Create a new file with the command:

items.html:
cd ~/picar-x/example
sudo nano test_tts_espeak.py

inlines.v: Then copy the example code into it. Press

items.code:
from picarx.tts import Espeak

tts = Espeak()

# Optional voice tuning
# tts.set_amp(100)   # 0 to 200
# tts.set_speed(150) # 80 to 260
# tts.set_gap(5)     # 0 to 200
# tts.set_pitch(50)  # 0 to 99

# Quick hello (sanity check)
tts.say("Hello! I'm Espeak TTS.")

Pico2Wave produces a more natural, human-like voice than Espeak. It's simpler to use but less flexible — you can only change the language, not the pitch or speed.
Create a new file with the command:

items.html:
cd ~/picar-x/example
sudo nano test_tts_pico2wave.py

inlines.v: Then copy the example code into it. Press

items.code:
from picarx.tts import Pico2Wave

tts = Pico2Wave()

tts.set_lang('en-US')  # en-US, en-GB, de-DE, es-ES, fr-FR, it-IT

# Quick hello (sanity check)
tts.say("Hello! I'm Pico2Wave TTS.")

cd ~/picar-x/example

inlines.v: Run this code and you'll see your PiCar-X drive forward, backward, and turn, each time announcing its move first. This makes your car safer, friendlier, and more interactive.

blocks.code:
from picarx import Picarx
from picarx.tts import Espeak
import time

# If you want to try Pico2Wave instead of Espeak, uncomment below:
# from picarx.tts import Pico2Wave
# tts = Pico2Wave()
# tts.set_lang('en-US')  # Options: en-US, en-GB, de-DE, es-ES, fr-FR, it-IT

px = Picarx()
tts = Espeak()

# Quick hello (test)
tts.say("Hello! I'm PiCar-X.")

def main():
    try:
        # Forward
        tts.say("Moving forward")
        px.forward(30)
        time.sleep(2)
        px.stop()

        # Backward
        tts.say("Moving backward")
        px.backward(30)
        time.sleep(2)
        px.stop()

        # Turn left
        tts.say("Turning left")
        px.set_dir_servo_angle(-20)
        px.forward(30)
        time.sleep(2)
        px.stop()
        px.set_dir_servo_angle(0)

        # Turn right
        tts.say("Turning right")
        px.set_dir_servo_angle(20)
        px.forward(30)
        time.sleep(2)
        px.stop()
        px.set_dir_servo_angle(0)

    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        # Stop if interrupted
        px.stop()
    finally:
        # Reset to safe state
        px.stop()
        px.set_dir_servo_angle(0)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

inlines.v: No sound when running Espeak or Pico2Wave
Check that your speakers/headphones are connected and volume is not muted.
Run a quick test in terminal:

items.code:
espeak "Hello world"
pico2wave -w test.wav "Hello world" && aplay test.wav
items.html:
espeak "Hello world"
pico2wave -w test.wav "Hello world" && aplay test.wav

inlines.v: If you hear nothing, the issue is with audio output, not your Python code.
Espeak voice sounds too fast or too robotic
Try adjusting the parameters in your code:

items.html:
tts.set_speed(120)   # slower
tts.set_pitch(60)    # different pitch
sudo python3 test_tts_espeak.py
